description_full: Lamar Advertising Company is one of the largest outdoor advertising companies in North America, with over 362,000 displays across the United States and Canada. Lamar offers advertisers a variety of billboards, interstate logo, transit and airport advertising formats, helping both local businesses and national brands reach broad audiences every day. In addition to its more traditional out-of-home inventory, Lamar is proud to offer its customers the largest network of digital billboards in the United States with over 5,400 displays. Lamar Advertising Company was founded and incorporated in 1902 in Delaware and is based in Baton Rouge, United States.
ceo_bio: Mr. Sean E. Reilly J.D. | CEO & President | Age 63 | Compensation: $2.6M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 3K people. Revenue per employee of $647K ranks in the bottom quartile among Real Estate peers. Each employee generates $195K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $10K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: Lamar Advertising Company is a large-cap real estate business with a $16.4B market cap on $2.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $683M in free cash flow — roughly 30 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.47× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.8×.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 34% operating margin runs 12pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 146 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 20% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 20% and a beta of 1.01, it moves roughly with the market.
About $76.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $157 (margin of safety -3%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $121 to $202 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $162 on average, in line with the price.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 8.9%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.42).
It converts 30% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.47x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 30%.
ROE of 58% is amplified by 6.9x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.0x net debt to EBITDA ($64.8M of cash against $3.4B of debt), with interest covered 4.8x.
The current ratio of 0.58 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.7% over 3 years and 7.6% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 6.1% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 8.7% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (8.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 36, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and institutions hold 99%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $4.9M sold).
It returns 4.4% a year to shareholders (0.9% in buybacks and 4.1% in dividends).
It pays out 113% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 3,500 employees, each generates about $647K of revenue, 0.3x the Real Estate median, and revenue has grown 4.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $195K of free cash flow per employee.
